verses.1: Al-Mizan reads the Mount most plausibly as Sinai, hallowed by God's speech to Moses, while recording the alternative of any blessed mountain. Of the proposed meanings of the inscribed Book on unrolled raqq, it prefers the Torah written on parchment over the Guarded Tablet, angels' deed-records, or the Qur'an; the Book's indefiniteness marks it as so well known that it is effectively definite. The greatly frequented House may be the Kaaba, though narrations identify a celestial house above it visited by angels; the raised vault is heaven. Masjūr may mean overflowing, but the commentary prefers blazing, supported by (81:6), while also reporting boiling seas. These oaths establish the foretold punishment of Judgement as an unavertable fixed decree, and calling it the Prophet's Lord reassures him of divine support against deniers.

verses.9: Al-Mizan cites al-Ṭabrisī's definition of mawr as alternating coming and going, like swirling smoke before it vanishes, and al-Rāghib's as rapid movement. The violently whirling sky thus depicts the celestial world being rolled up, as in (82:1–2), (21:104), and (39:67). The mountains' awful motion depicts the earth's quake at the Final Hour, when they are shattered and dispersed as dust or become a mirage ((56:6); (78:20)).

verses.11: Al-Mizan presents (52:11), (52:12), and (52:13) as the chapter’s central warning: because the punishment of the Day of Judgement is inescapable, woe belongs to the deniers who still deny it. Although the verse does not expressly mention hellfire, wayl implies that destiny. Alternatively, the wording says that the certain punishment can fall only on those who rejected God, the Resurrection, and the Prophet’s summons. Their khawḍ is false speech—originally ‘delving,’ and here perhaps ‘strange vain talk’—and calling it play shows that argument, denial, and mockery of God’s signs yield only delusive results. Their forcible driving to hell expounds ‘that day.’ Al-Mizan reads the Fire of (52:14) as the manifested confirmation of the revelation conveyed by the Prophets, which the guilty denied. The rebuke of (52:15) consequently says that a Fire now plainly seen and undergone proves that the miracles and revelation dismissed as magic or invention were neither. Iṣlaw–hā commands exposure to the Fire’s heat. Patience and impatience make no difference because neither endurance nor panic can lessen or escape an inevitable requital inseparable from one’s earthly deeds. For the Godwary, jannāt are shaded gardens and naʿīm an abundance of blessings. Fākihīn may describe their speaking of God’s gifts, sharing their fruits, enjoying His generosity, or being amazed by it; the repeated ‘their Lord’ displays His special concern in saving them from hell. In (52:19), hanīʾan may be an absolute object or a direct object: their food and drink may be the reward of their deeds, or their enjoyment of them may be that reward. Muttakiʾīn depicts resting on cushions upon raised, side-by-side couches. ‘We will wed’ means pairing them with houris, not solemnising marriage: wa zawwajnā-hum bi-ḥūr-i ʿayn uses bi in a way the ordinary doubly transitive sense of marrying does not. Al-Mizan distinguishes ittibāʿ, which entails imitating the one followed, from luhūq, which only brings people to the same destination. God’s blessing is to join faithful descendants to their forebears in Paradise even when their faith is less intense, without diminishing the parents’ reward. The unqualified descendants most directly means adults capable of faith, not minors, without contradicting the doctrine that minor children of believers are presumed believers. A possible reading drawn from the indefinite īmān also includes children who followed their parents while young; then the pronouns in ‘We will not stint them’ concern the parents, whose reward cannot be reduced for their children’s admission. Al-Mizan rejects as ill-informed the readings that make ‘the faithful’ an object of the preceding ‘wed,’ restrict descendants to minors, or make the pronouns refer to descendants receiving their full good or bad recompense before joining their parents. ‘Every man is a hostage’ (rahīn) explains why no one’s earned recompense can be transferred: like collateral held for a debt, each person remains held for full repayment in reward or punishment. The different context of ‘Every soul is hostage … except the People of the Right Hand’ concerns captivity to punishment. Al-Mizan also notes the proposal that the present phrase is an aside about hell’s inmates, and al-Zamakhsharī’s figurative account of a servant held for required works, but finds the latter insufficient to explain its link with the verse. Amdadnā-hum, from imdād, denotes repeated provision and is used for good, unlike madd for evil; Paradise therefore supplies desired fruits and meat without ceasing. A kaʾs is necessarily a wine cup, but its wine produces neither the vain talk (laghw) nor the sinful conduct (taʾthīm) of worldly drink. The ghilmān who circulate in service are, according to a reported explanation, not former earthly servants but beautiful, pure creatures of Paradise like guarded pearls. The blessed then ask one another about their former condition and the path to this felicity. Their fī ahlinā mushfiqīn expresses fearful, loving concern for their families: they lived graciously with them, advised them, and called them away from error. Their salvation is God’s favor, mann, poured out as mercy, and rescue from al-samūm; al-Ṭabrisī explains this as heat that penetrates the body’s pores and pains it. Their former supplication meant worshipping God’s oneness, obeying Him, and guiding their families toward truth. Al-Mizan therefore connects their mercy and deliverance to those practices, while locating their ultimate source in God as al-Birr, the All-benign who treats His servants kindly, and al-Raḥīm, the All-merciful.

verses.14: Al-Mizan says that the Fire is the confirmation, now made manifest, of the prophetic revelation that the guilty denied: it proves both its existence and God’s promised punishment for them.
verses.15: Al-Mizan reads the question as a rebuke: the Fire directly seen and experienced disproves the deniers’ claim that the Prophets’ miracles and revelation were magic, trickery, or fiction.
verses.16: Al-Mizan explains iṣlaw–hā as the command to submit to the Fire’s heat. Whether the condemned are patient or impatient, neither endurance nor alarm can lessen or avert it; this unchangeable outcome is their recompense for deeds from which they cannot be separated.
verses.17: Al-Mizan says the Godwary will inhabit shaded gardens and an abundance of bliss. Fākihīn may mean speaking of God’s gifts, sharing fruits, enjoying His generosity, or marvelling at it; repeating ‘their Lord’ underscores His great care in saving them from hell.
verses.18: Al-Mizan says the Godwary will inhabit shaded gardens and an abundance of bliss. Fākihīn may mean speaking of God’s gifts, sharing fruits, enjoying His generosity, or marvelling at it; repeating ‘their Lord’ underscores His great care in saving them from hell.
verses.19: Al-Mizan explains that hanīʾan can mean either ‘eat and drink enjoyably’ or ‘enjoyable food and drink.’ Accordingly, ‘for what you used to do’ may make the food itself the result of earthly deeds, or make the enjoyment of it their result.
verses.20: Al-Mizan takes muttakiʾīn as resting on cushions and surur maṣfūfa as raised couches arranged side by side. ‘We will wed them’ means that they are paired with houris, not that a marriage is solemnised: wa zawwajnā-hum bi-ḥūr-i ʿayn uses bi unlike the ordinary doubly transitive sense of marrying.
verses.21:
Al-Mizan distinguishes ittibāʿ, following by imitation, from luhūq, merely reaching the same destination. God’s blessing is to join descendants who follow their faithful forebears with any degree of faith, even a lower degree, without diminishing the parents’ reward. Most directly, the unqualified descendants are adults capable of faith, not children who died as minors, though this does not deny the doctrine that minor children of believers are presumed believers. A possible reading of the indefinite īmān includes those who followed their parents while young; in that case, ‘We will not stint them’ still concerns the parents and removes any thought that their reward purchases their children’s admission.

Al-Mizan rejects as ill-informed readings that make ‘the faithful’ an object of the preceding ‘wed,’ limit descendants to minors, or make the pronouns refer to descendants who first receive full recompense and are then joined to their parents. ‘Every man is a hostage’ (rahīn) grounds the promise: as collateral is held for a debt, every person is held for the full recompense of his own good or evil deeds, so none can be transferred to another. The hostagehood of the People of the Right Hand in (74:38–39) concerns punishment in its own context. Al-Mizan mentions an interpretation making this an aside about hell’s inmates and al-Zamakhsharī’s figurative account of a servant held for required works, but finds the latter unable to explain the phrase’s connection here.
verses.22: Al-Mizan says amdadnā-hum, from imdād, means repeatedly bringing a good thing, unlike madd, which is used for evil. The inhabitants of Paradise will therefore receive desired fruits and meats again and again without cessation.
verses.23: Al-Mizan explains yatanāzaʿūn as gathering and passing a kaʾs, a large cup that in classical Arabic contains wine. Its freedom from laghw and taʾthīm confirms that it is wine, but wine of the hereafter has none of the vain speech or sinful conduct caused by worldly drinking.
verses.24: Al-Mizan takes yaṭūf here as coming and going in service. A reported explanation says the indefinite ghilmānin lahum are not their former earthly servants but, like the houris, beautiful, graceful, pure creatures of Paradise, likened to guarded pearls.
verses.25: Al-Mizan says the inhabitants of Paradise ask one another about their former condition and what led them to its blessings.
verses.26: Al-Mizan, following al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, defines ishfāq as concern joined to fear; with fī it particularly stresses fearfulness. The blessed recall caring for their families’ happiness and rescue from error, living graciously with them, advising them, and calling them to truth.
verses.27: Al-Mizan explains mann as the pouring out of blessings, praiseworthy from God though blameworthy when people enumerate favors. God favored the inhabitants of Paradise through mercy, felicity, and rescue from al-samūm; al-Ṭabrisī identifies it as painful heat that penetrates the pores, as a hot wind does.
verses.28: Al-Mizan says their former supplication—worshipping God’s oneness, obeying Him, and drawing their families toward truth—explains the favor and rescue from al-samūm described in the preceding verses. Their care for family belongs to the same pattern. Its ultimate source is God as al-Birr, the All-benign who treats kindly, and al-Raḥīm, the All-merciful; the passage compares this pattern with (103:2–3).
verses.29: Al-Mizan takes the command to admonish as the conclusion drawn from the deniers’ coming punishment and the Godwary’s protection in bliss: the Prophet warns with truth and is neither soothsayer nor mad. ‘By your Lord’s blessing’ does not merely deny attributes absent from most people; it points to the many divine favors that make their ascription to him inconceivable.
verses.30: Al-Mizan explains tarabbaṣ as awaiting a reversal of fortune and rayb al-manūn as anxiety about death. The deniers call the Prophet a poet whose death they expect will erase his message and leave them at ease.
verses.31: Al-Mizan says the Prophet is told to answer their waiting with his own. The command is a threat: what they await will indeed come, but it will be their ruin and everlasting punishment, not relief from his message.
verses.32: Al-Mizan reads aḥlām as intellects and ‘this’ as the deniers’ words and expectation that the Prophet will perish. The question exposes the absurdity of answering truth with such falsehood; it is their rebelliousness, not intellect, that prompts it.
verses.33: Al-Mizan, citing al-Ṭabrisī, says taqawwal denotes tortuous and therefore false speech. The deniers accuse the Prophet of fabricating the Qurʾan and falsely attributing it to God; the verse answers that their lack of faith drives this accusation.
verses.34: Al-Mizan treats the challenge to bring a discourse like the Qurʾan as the direct answer to the charge that the Prophet fabricated it. If it were ordinary human speech, they could produce its like; their inability demonstrates its miraculous inimitability and that it is God’s speech. This can also refute their charges of soothsaying, madness, poetry, and fabrication, though the direct reply to fabrication is closest to the wording.
verses.35: Al-Mizan takes ‘created from something else’ to mean created unlike the rest of humankind, as though the deniers alone had no divine duties, commands, prohibitions, or recompense because messengers were sent only to everyone else. It judges this reading the closest and most comprehensive, while noting alternatives: created without a maker, from inanimate matter, without a purpose of reward and punishment, or in vain. ‘Or are they creators?’ asks whether they created themselves and thus need neither God’s care nor His commands.
verses.36: Al-Mizan explains the question as asking whether the deniers created the heavens and earth and are therefore gods or lords too exalted to serve another. The answer is that they possess no certainty.
verses.37: Al-Mizan asks whether the deniers own God’s treasuries and may therefore assign or withhold prophethood, or possess dominion over God and can take back the Prophethood and messengership He gave the Prophet. Muṣayṭirūn derives from sayṭara, power and dominion.
verses.38: Al-Mizan explains sullam as a stepped ladder, yastamiʿūn as eavesdropping with the sense of ascent, and sulṭān as decisive proof. The verse asks whether the deniers ascend to heaven to hear revelation, select what to accept, and reject the rest; if so, their alleged listener must produce manifest authority.
verses.39: Al-Mizan reports that the question mocks the deniers for assigning daughters to God while preferring sons for themselves.
verses.40: Al-Mizan explains maghram through ghurm, a loss of property not caused by crime or betrayal, and muthaqlūn as people burdened with difficulty. The verse asks whether the Prophet demands payment for his message, so that its debt weighs them down.
verses.41: Al-Mizan reports readings of the Unseen as the Guarded Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ), from which the deniers allegedly transcribe certain knowledge about the Prophet; as unseen knowledge generally, recorded as a code for others; and of ‘write’ as passing judgement.
verses.42: Al-Mizan defines kayd as a stratagem or concealed plot. In context, the deniers seek to thwart the Prophet by calling him a soothsayer, madman, poet, or fabricator and turning people from him; they thereby plot against themselves, losing eternal happiness, while God outmaneuvers them by withholding divine success and sealing their hearts. It reports the specific Dār al-Nadwa and Badr interpretation, which would make the verse a prophecy, but finds it unsuited to this passage’s context and tone.
verses.43: Al-Mizan says that if the deniers had another creator and guardian, they could dispense with Allah, reject His Messenger, and seek that god’s protection from the threatened punishment. The verse instead declares Allah exalted above every partner they ascribe to Him.
verses.44: Al-Mizan explains kisf as a fragment and markūm as piled together. The deniers’ obstinacy is so deep that even a piece of sky falling on their heads would be dismissed as a cumulous cloud, not recognised as a sign of divine punishment; the passage likens this to (15:14–15).
verses.45:
Al-Mizan explains dhar–hum as the command to leave the deniers alone. Having met and exhausted their excuses, the Prophet is told to abandon people so obstinate that they would explain away the clearest sign; this is also a quiet warning of the punishment that will engulf them. Their day of yuṣʿaqūn most aptly means the sounding of the Trumpet, one of the End Times’ signs, when those in heaven and earth pass away (39:68). The following description—that no guile or help will avail—fits the Day of Resurrection, where all means fail and command belongs to God.

Al-Mizan answers the objection that these deniers will already have died by holding that those in Barzakh also die when the Trumpet sounds. It allows that ‘they’ may instead mean those alive then and that the threat is punishment on that day. It finds the Battle of Badr reading unlikely and the reading of their individual death incompatible with the chapter’s warning of Judgement. The additional punishment for wrongdoers is not unlikely to be ʿadhāb al-qabr; ‘most of them do not know’ suggests that some know yet obstinately persist. The Badr interpretation of this punishment does not fit the verse’s ending.
verses.46:
Al-Mizan explains dhar–hum as the command to leave the deniers alone. Having met and exhausted their excuses, the Prophet is told to abandon people so obstinate that they would explain away the clearest sign; this is also a quiet warning of the punishment that will engulf them. Their day of yuṣʿaqūn most aptly means the sounding of the Trumpet, one of the End Times’ signs, when those in heaven and earth pass away (39:68). The following description—that no guile or help will avail—fits the Day of Resurrection, where all means fail and command belongs to God.

Al-Mizan answers the objection that these deniers will already have died by holding that those in Barzakh also die when the Trumpet sounds. It allows that ‘they’ may instead mean those alive then and that the threat is punishment on that day. It finds the Battle of Badr reading unlikely and the reading of their individual death incompatible with the chapter’s warning of Judgement. The additional punishment for wrongdoers is not unlikely to be ʿadhāb al-qabr; ‘most of them do not know’ suggests that some know yet obstinately persist. The Badr interpretation of this punishment does not fit the verse’s ending.

verses.48:
Al-Mizan says that the Lord’s judgement appears to be His temporary respite and sealing of the deniers’ hearts, together with His command that the Prophet continue calling to truth despite persecution. ‘You fare before Our eyes’ most fittingly means that God sees his whole condition and has not forgotten him, strengthening the call to patience and intensified preaching; the alternative reading, that the Prophet is under God’s guard, is less suited to the context.

The commentary reports al-Ṭabrisī’s seven readings of ‘when you rise’: rising from sleep, from a nap connected with ṣalāt al-ẓuhr, from a gathering, any rising, rising for obligatory prayer, rising for any prayer, or the two units before morning prayer. Glorifying God at night refers to night prayers, though some say the sunset and evening prayers, ṣalāt al-maghrib and ṣalāt al-ʿishāʾ. The receding stars may mean their disappearance at daybreak and thus the two pre-dawn units, the morning prayer itself, or continual morning-and-evening remembrance.
